title: No. 18 — The Same Subject Continued (The Insufficiency of the Present Confederation to Preserve the Union) For the New York Packet. Friday, (Hamilton & Madison)
paragraphs: MADISON, with HAMILTON

Among the confederacies of antiquity, the most significant was that of the Greek republics joined under the Amphictyonic council. From the best surviving accounts of this celebrated institution, it offers a very instructive parallel to the present Confederation of the American States.

Its members kept the character of independent and sovereign states, and they had equal votes in the federal council. This council had a general authority to propose and decide whatever it judged necessary for the common welfare of Greece. It could declare and wage war, settle all controversies between members as a final court, fine the aggressor, deploy the whole force of the confederacy against any disobedient party, and admit new members. The Amphictyons were guardians of religion and of the immense riches belonging to the temple of Delphos, where they had jurisdiction over disputes between the inhabitants and visitors who came to consult the oracle. To make the federal powers more effective, they swore a mutual oath to defend and protect the united cities, to punish those who broke this oath, and to take vengeance on anyone who profaned the temple.

In theory, and on paper, this set of powers seems entirely sufficient for any general purpose. In several important respects they go beyond the powers listed in our articles of confederation. The Amphictyons controlled the superstition of their age, one of the chief tools of government at that time. They had a declared authority to use force against rebellious cities, and they were sworn to use that authority whenever necessary.

The experiment, however, was very different from the theory. The powers, like those of our present Congress, were administered by deputies appointed by the cities in their political capacities, and were exercised over those cities in the same capacities. The result was weakness, disorder, and finally the destruction of the confederacy. The more powerful members, instead of being kept in check, took turns tyrannizing over all the rest. According to Demosthenes, Athens was master of Greece for seventy-three years. The Lacedaemonians ruled it next for twenty-nine years. After the battle of Leuctra, the Thebans had their turn at domination.
It happened all too often, according to Plutarch, that the deputies of the strongest cities intimidated and corrupted those of the weaker, and judgment then went in favor of the most powerful party.

Even during defensive and dangerous wars with Persia and Macedon, the members never acted together. More or fewer of them were always either dupes or paid agents of the common enemy. The intervals between foreign wars were filled with domestic upheavals, convulsions, and slaughter.

After the war with Xerxes ended, the Lacedaemonians demanded that several cities be expelled from the confederacy for the disloyal part they had played. The Athenians, seeing that this measure would cost the Lacedaemonians fewer allies than themselves, and would make them masters of the public deliberations, vigorously opposed and defeated the attempt. This piece of history shows at once the inefficiency of the union, the ambition and jealousy of its most powerful members, and the dependent and degraded condition of the rest. The smaller members, though entitled in theory to revolve in equal pride and majesty around the common center, had become in fact mere satellites of the larger bodies.

Had the Greeks been as wise as they were brave, says the Abbe Milot, experience would have taught them the necessity of a closer union. They would have used the peace that followed their victory over the Persians to put such a reform in place. Instead of this obvious policy, Athens and Sparta, swollen by the victories and glory they had won, became first rivals and then enemies. They did each other infinitely more harm than they had suffered from Xerxes. Their mutual jealousies, fears, hatreds, and injuries ended in the famous Peloponnesian war, which ended in the ruin and slavery of the Athenians who had begun it.

A weak government, even when not at war, is constantly shaken by internal divisions, and these never fail to bring fresh disasters from abroad. When the Phocians plowed up some consecrated ground belonging to the temple of Apollo, the Amphictyonic council, true to the superstition of the age, fined the sacrilegious offenders. Backed by Athens and Sparta, the Phocians refused to obey the decree. The Thebans, with several other cities, undertook to uphold the Amphictyons' authority and avenge the offended god. Being the weaker party, they invited the help of Philip of Macedon, who had secretly fueled the conflict. Philip eagerly seized the chance to carry out the plans he had long laid against the liberties of Greece. Through his intrigues and bribes he won over the popular leaders of several cities. By their influence and votes he gained admission to the Amphictyonic council, and through his cunning and his armies he made himself master of the confederacy.

Such were the consequences of the false principle on which this remarkable institution was founded. Had Greece been bound by a stricter confederation and persevered in her union, says one shrewd observer of her fate, she would never have worn the chains of Macedon, and might have proved a barrier to the vast designs of Rome.
The Achaean league, as it is called, was another association of Greek republics, and it gives us valuable instruction.
The Union here was far closer, and its organization much wiser, than in the previous case. As a result, although it did not escape a similar disaster, it certainly did not equally deserve one.

The cities making up this league kept their own municipal jurisdiction, appointed their own officers, and enjoyed perfect equality. The senate, in which they were represented, had the sole and exclusive right to make peace and war, to send and receive ambassadors, to enter into treaties and alliances, and to appoint a chief magistrate, or praetor. He commanded their armies and, with the advice and consent of ten senators, not only ran the government when the senate was not in session but had a major share in its deliberations when it was. The original constitution provided two praetors who shared the administration, but in practice a single one was preferred.

It appears that all the cities had the same laws and customs, the same weights and measures, and the same money. How far this came from the federal council's authority is unclear. It is only said that the cities were in a way compelled to receive the same laws and usages. When Lacedaemon was brought into the league by Philopoemen, this was accompanied by the abolition of the institutions and laws of Lycurgus, and the adoption of those of the Achaeans. The Amphictyonic confederacy, of which she had been a member, had left her in full enjoyment of her own government and laws. This single fact proves a very real difference in the spirit of the two systems.

It is much to be regretted that only such imperfect records of this curious political fabric remain. If its inner structure and regular workings could be known, it would probably shed more light on the science of federal government than any of the similar experiments we are familiar with.

One important fact seems to be confirmed by every historian who notices Achaean affairs. Both after the league was renewed by Aratus, and before its dissolution by the arts of Macedon, there was infinitely more moderation and justice in the administration of its government, and far less violence and sedition among its people, than in any of the cities exercising all the prerogatives of sovereignty alone. The Abbe Mably, in his observations on Greece, says that popular government, which was so stormy elsewhere, caused no disorders within the Achaean republic, BECAUSE IT WAS THERE TEMPERED BY THE GENERAL AUTHORITY AND LAWS OF THE CONFEDERACY.

We must not, however, conclude too quickly that faction did not disturb individual cities to some degree, much less that proper subordination and harmony reigned in the system as a whole. The opposite is sufficiently shown by the upheavals and the fate of the republic.

While the Amphictyonic confederacy lasted, that of the Achaeans, which included only the lesser cities, made little figure on the Greek stage. When the former fell to Macedon, the latter was spared by the policy of Philip and Alexander. Under the successors of these princes, however, a different policy prevailed. The arts of division were practiced on the Achaeans. Each city was lured into a separate interest, and the union dissolved. Some cities fell under Macedonian garrisons; others under usurpers who sprang from their own confusion. Shame and oppression soon awakened their love of liberty. A few cities reunited. Their example was followed by others as opportunities arose to cut down their tyrants. The league soon embraced almost the entire Peloponnesus. Macedon saw its progress but was prevented by internal dissensions from stopping it. All Greece caught the enthusiasm and seemed ready to join in one confederacy. Then jealousy and envy in Sparta and Athens of the rising glory of the Achaeans threw a fatal damper on the project. The fear of Macedonian power led the league to seek alliance with the kings of Egypt and Syria, who, as successors of Alexander, were rivals of the king of Macedon. This policy was defeated by Cleomenes, king of Sparta, whose ambition led him to make an unprovoked attack on his Achaean neighbors. As an enemy of Macedon, Cleomenes had enough influence with the Egyptian and Syrian princes to break their commitments to the league.

The Achaeans were now reduced to the dilemma of submitting to Cleomenes or begging help from Macedon, their former oppressor. They chose the latter. The quarrels of the Greeks always gave that powerful neighbor a welcome chance to meddle in their affairs. A Macedonian army quickly arrived. Cleomenes was defeated. The Achaeans soon learned, as so often happens, that a victorious and powerful ally is just another name for a master. The most they could obtain by their most submissive compliance was permission to keep their own laws. Philip, now on the throne of Macedon, by his tyrannies soon provoked fresh combinations among the Greeks. The Achaeans, though weakened by internal dissensions and by the revolt of Messene, one of their members, raised the standard of opposition with the Aetolians and Athenians joining them. Finding that even with this support they were not strong enough, they once more resorted to the dangerous expedient of bringing in foreign arms. The Romans, when invited, eagerly accepted. Philip was conquered and Macedon subdued. A new crisis followed for the league. Dissensions broke out among its members. The Romans encouraged these. Callicrates and other popular leaders became hired tools to mislead their countrymen. To feed discord and disorder more effectively, the Romans, to the astonishment of those who trusted their sincerity, had already proclaimed universal liberty (1) throughout Greece. With the same treacherous design they now lured members away from the league by appealing to their pride about violations of their sovereignty. By such tactics this union, the last hope of Greece and of ancient liberty, was torn apart. So much weakness and confusion were introduced that Roman arms had little trouble completing the ruin which Roman cunning had begun. The Achaeans were cut to pieces, and Achaia loaded with the chains under which it groans to this hour.

I have not thought it superfluous to give the outlines of this important piece of history. It teaches more than one lesson. As a supplement to the outlines of the Achaean constitution, it strikingly shows how federal bodies tend toward anarchy among the members rather than tyranny at the head.
1. This was just another, more flattering name for the independence of the members from the federal head.
